title: The LORD Roars from Zion
sum: Amos introduces himself, dates his words by two kings and an earthquake, and gives the motto of the book: the LORD roars from Zion. Then he begins to speak against Israel's neighbors. Five nations are named in this chapter, Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom and Ammon, and Moab, Judah and Israel follow in chapter 2. Each has the same opening, "For three rebellions of X, and for four, I will not turn it back", the same crime (a cruelty done to others) and the same punishment: fire on the walls.
The crowd at Bethel would have agreed with every word. These were their enemies. The pattern is a trap that closes in chapter 2, where Judah and then Israel are named in exactly the same form.

views.H: The cruelties are war crimes of the 9th and 8th centuries: Hazael's campaigns in Gilead (2 Kings 10:32-33; 13:3-7), the Philistine and Tyrian slave trade, Edom's long hatred, Ammon's raids on Gilead. Amos is dated by Uzziah, Jeroboam II and an earthquake that some excavators think they can see at Hazor.
views.C: Wolff, Jeremias and others suspect later hands in 1:9-12 (Tyre and Edom, with their "brothers" language) and in the motto of 1:2, which also stands in Joel 3:16. Paul and Andersen-Freedman defend most of it for Amos. The "three and four" pattern is a known form (Proverbs 30).
views.J: In later rabbinic writing Edom became a name for Rome, which colors the Jewish reading of 1:11-12; Radak instead ties the Edom oracle to the destruction of the Second Temple. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra place the earthquake of 1:1 on the day King Uzziah went into the Temple to burn incense (Ibn Ezra adds that this is tradition and not Scripture). Radak reads the roar of 1:2 as a figure for prophecy, and the Targum Jonathan has the LORD "lift up his word" from Jerusalem.
views.X: Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret and Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote commentaries on the Twelve, and Calvin lectured on them. Christian readers have used the chapter to show that God judges every nation by how it treats others.
views.F: Futurist readers who take the oracles as history generally place the fire of 1:4-14 in the 8th and 7th centuries; some dispensational writers see a pattern for judgment on the nations at the end.

deep.h: The shape of the nation oracles
deep.b:
Eight oracles run in a ring around Israel (seven against peoples, Judah among them, and the eighth against Israel itself): Damascus (northeast), Gaza (southwest), Tyre (northwest), Edom (southeast), Ammon (east), Moab (southeast), Judah (south), and then Israel itself. The first seven have the same parts: a messenger formula ("The LORD says this"), the number formula, a charge, and the fire (1:4, 7, 10, 12, 14; 2:2, 5). Israel's oracle has no fire; it ends in a day of battle (2:13-16). From 2:4 the form changes: Judah gets no named cruelty, and Israel gets a long list. Most commentators read the series as a net drawn tight, as in a sermon that wins the crowd's agreement before turning on it.

The crimes are all done to people, not to the LORD directly. Damascus and Ammon destroy the weak in war; Gaza and Tyre sell whole communities; Edom abandons kinship; Moab desecrates a dead king. The standard of judgment is the same for all nations, and it is not the Law of Moses. That is why the closing oracles against Judah and Israel matter: they are judged by the law they were given as well (2:4).

deep.title: The ring and the eye
deep.b: My own reading, which overlaps with the "encirclement" described by Wolff and Paul: the eight oracles read like an eye turning round a compass. Starting at Damascus, the northeast neighbor of Israel, the list goes to the southwest, the northwest, the southeast, the east, the southeast again and then the south, and ends in the middle. No nation is named twice and no direction is left out. If this is on purpose, it would mean Amos was building a picture of the world as Israel saw it, with Israel at its center, and then taking that center apart. This is a pattern in the text; it is a theory that it was intended.

echoes: Joel 3:16; Jeremiah 49:27; Jeremiah 49:2-3; Proverbs 30:15-33; 2 Kings 10:32-33; 2 Kings 13:3-7; Obadiah 10-14; Genesis 25:23

settings.by: The editor who set Amos's words in a book; the motto (1:2) is presented as Amos's
settings.to: Whoever read the book later, in Israel and in Judah
settings.when: The book gives the time as two years before the earthquake, in the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam II (about 760 BC)
settings.why: To name the man, the times and the shape of what follows: the LORD is a lion who roars from Jerusalem, in a book that mostly speaks to the north. The title fixes Amos in Judah's history and the north's.
settings.readers: To the book's first readers, who knew the earthquake and what came after it (Assyria and the fall of Samaria), the date was a mark that the words had come true.
views: Amos wrote or spoke the motto
Paul and Andersen-Freedman treat 1:2 as the opening of Amos's own preaching.
Wolff and Jeremias think 1:1-2 come from editors after Amos, who wanted the lion's roar from Zion to frame the book (compare Joel 3:16).

settings.by: Amos, speaking as the LORD's messenger ("The LORD says this")
settings.to: The people of the northern kingdom, probably gathered at a festival at Bethel, with Judah in the background (see 7:10-13)
settings.when: The reign of Jeroboam II, in a time of peace and wealth; the exact event is not given, and 7:10-13 puts Amos at Bethel
settings.why: To win the listeners' agreement by condemning their enemies, and then to condemn them by the same standard. Without knowing the audience, the oracles look like a list of foreign news; knowing it, they are a trap.
settings.readers: For the readers of the book after 722 BC, who knew that the fire had reached Samaria too, the oracles showed that the LORD's judgment on Israel was no different from his judgment on others.
views: Most scholars imagine the first hearing as a public speech at the shrine of Bethel at a festival (Wolff, Paul).
Some think the series is a literary piece that was never spoken as such (compare Jeremias).

title: Moab, Judah and Israel
sum: The series reaches its last three oracles. Moab burns the bones of Edom's king. Judah, which has no named cruelty, has "rejected the LORD's teaching". And then, with the same words, the LORD names Israel. The list of Israel's crimes is long and exact: selling the poor over small debts, trampling heads in the dust, a father and son with the same young woman, coats kept as pledges, wine from fines.

The LORD reminds Israel what he did for it: he wiped out the Amorites, brought Israel out of Egypt and gave it prophets and Nazirites. Israel gave the Nazirites wine and told the prophets to be quiet. The chapter ends with a day of battle in which no one escapes.

views.H: The charges match the economy of the 8th century: land and debt, the sale of people for small sums (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5 shows a later form), shrine meals paid for by fines. The prophets whom Israel silenced are an early sign of the clash with Amaziah in 7:10-17.
views.C: The Judah oracle (2:4-5) is the most argued: no deed is named, and its language is that of the Deuteronomic editors. If it is an addition, the original series ended with Israel as the seventh oracle at the climax. 2:9-12 also looks like a Deuteronomic expansion to some (Wolff); others see it as part of Amos.
views.J: Rashi and the Targum say Moab burned the bones of Edom's king and plastered the walls of a house with the lime as an insult (2:1). Radak ties that crime to 2 Kings 3:27, and Ibn Ezra reports the same link as one view. The Torah laws on the coat in pledge (Exodus 22:26; Deuteronomy 24:12-13) and the Nazirite (Numbers 6) stand behind 2:8 and 2:11-12.
views.X: Christian writers have read 2:6-8 as a root of the church's teaching on the poor. Catholic social teaching, Anabaptist and liberation writers all cite 2:6-7.
views.F: Few futurist readings concern this chapter; "that day" in 2:16 is the day of the battle, not the end of the world.

deep.h: What does each crime say about Israel?
deep.b:
The six charges in 2:6-8 are a short course in the covenant law that was broken. Selling the poor (2:6) breaks the rules on debt slavery (Exodus 21:2-11; Leviticus 25:39-43). Trampling the poor (2:7) is the denial of justice in the gate (compare 5:12). Father and son with the same young woman (2:7) is sexual exploitation, and may break the laws of Leviticus 18; the text does not say. Coats kept as pledges (2:8) breaks Exodus 22:26-27. Wine from fines (2:8) is profit from unjust fines. Each time the victim is someone who cannot answer.

2:7 says these acts "profane my holy name". The point is that the way people are treated is a matter of the LORD's own honor, not only of ethics.

echoes: Exodus 21:2-11; Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-13; Leviticus 18:8, 15; Numbers 6:1-21; Judges 13:5; 2 Kings 3:26-27; Amos 5:12; Amos 8:6

settings.to: The people of Israel (and the powerful who run the courts and the markets), the same audience as 1:3-2:5
settings.when: During Jeroboam II's peace; in the series after Judah
settings.why: To say to the listeners, who have cheered at the fire on their neighbors, that the same fire is for them, and to do it by naming the very acts they do daily. The LORD's gifts in 2:9-11 are the background: they owe him.
settings.readers: For readers after 722 BC the list explained why Samaria fell: not a strange accident but the judgment named in advance.
views: Most scholars take 2:6-16 as the climax of one speech with 1:3-2:5.
Wolff and others think 2:9-12 was written in the style of the Deuteronomic school.

title: You Only Have I Known
sum: The first of three sermons that begin "Hear this word". It opens with the LORD's claim on Israel: "You are the only ones I have known among all the clans of the earth. That is why I will call you to account for all your guilt." Then comes a run of questions about cause and effect, a lion, a bird, a trap, a ram's horn, and a city. The answer to the last one is that disaster comes from the LORD; and the LORD does nothing without telling his prophets.

The second half calls Ashdod and Egypt to look on Samaria and see the oppression inside it. The sermon ends with a shepherd's scrap, the altars of Bethel cut down, and the winter and summer houses struck.

views.H: Samaria in the 8th century was rich: ivory furnishings are attested at the site (3:15; 6:4); the separate winter and summer houses of 3:15 are known only from Amos. Calling Ashdod and Egypt as witnesses recalls the powers whose armies could reach the hill of Samaria.
views.C: 3:7 is often seen as an addition in the Deuteronomic style (Wolff). 3:1 may have been extended by editors to include "the whole clan" and the exodus. The questions in 3:3-8 are seen as a piece of wisdom teaching that Amos uses.
views.J: The Talmud cites 3:2 to explain why Israel is judged more strictly than the nations (Avodah Zarah 4a). The question "Does disaster fall on a city and the LORD has not done it?" is read against the background of the LORD's justice. Rashi takes "know" in 3:2 as "love", and Radak and Ibn Ezra compare a king who is angrier at the servants who stand before him than at strangers.
views.X: Christian readers have used 3:2 for the doctrine of election (Calvin's general and special election) and for the idea that privilege brings responsibility. 3:7 has been used by writers on prophecy and revelation.
views.F: Not a futurist chapter; the "day" is the day Samaria's altars are struck (3:14).

deep.b:
Seven questions fill 3:3-6. Each has the pattern "Does X happen unless Y?" and each expects the answer "no". In order: two walkers need an appointment, a lion roars only over prey, a bird falls only into a set snare, a trap springs only when it has caught something, a ram's horn alarms people, and disaster comes to a city only when the LORD has done it. The sequence moves from normal events to the one in question. The point of 3:7-8 is that the prophet's speaking is as sure a sign of the LORD's speaking as the lion's roar is of the prey.

It is debated whether the chain is Amos's answer to those who said he had no right to speak (compare 7:12-13), or a teaching form he borrowed from wisdom schools. Either way the last link leads straight to the point: a prophet who has heard the LORD cannot stay silent (3:8).

echoes: Genesis 18:19; Deuteronomy 7:6-8; Hosea 13:5; Jeremiah 1:5; Jeremiah 23:18; Exodus 22:13; 1 Kings 12:28-33; 1 Kings 22:39; Isaiah 45:7; Lamentations 3:38

traditions.q: What does "You only have I known" say about God's choice of Israel, and about his people today? (3:2)
views: Calvin separates the "general election" of the whole nation of Israel from the "special election" of those who are saved (Institutes 3.21.5-7). Being "known" brought the whole nation privilege and a heavier judgment. Election itself is by grace alone and not for merit (Westminster Confession 3).

Israel's election is a calling to serve and witness. The Church teaches that God's gifts and call to the Jewish people are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4, quoting Romans 11:29) and that the Church is the new People of God drawn from Jews and Gentiles (Lumen Gentium 9).

Wesley rejected unconditional election and taught that God calls all people and that the call can be refused. On this reading, Israel's being "known" was a privilege to be answered with obedience, not a guarantee. (Wesley does not comment on Amos 3:2; this applies his teaching on election to the verse.)

The Orthodox Church has no statement on this verse. In general it reads Israel's calling as a service fulfilled in Christ and the Church, and the Fathers warn that privilege without obedience brings judgment (a short summary; no source is cited).

The Baptist confessions speak of election to salvation and not of the nation of Israel, and they do not comment on Amos 3:2 (London Baptist Confession 1689, chapter 3; Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article V). Baptist readers of the verse generally see national privilege that carries responsibility (a short summary).

Election is election in Christ, made known in the gospel and not to be searched out in God's hidden will (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI). The verse is read as law: the more God has given, the more he asks. (The Formula does not comment on Amos 3:2; this applies its teaching to the verse.)
Israel's election is national and permanent, and is not replaced by the church; "you only have I known" marks Israel as the people to whom the earthly promises belong (Ryrie).

settings.to: "The Israelites, the whole clan" brought out of Egypt, that is the northern kingdom first, and (3:1) possibly Judah as well; in 3:9 the call goes out to Ashdod and Egypt to look on Samaria
settings.when: During Jeroboam II's peace, perhaps at Bethel
settings.why: To hold the people to their election: if the LORD alone has known them, he alone can call them to account. The chain of questions argues that the prophet speaks because the LORD has spoken. The call to the foreign citadels turns the crime into something visible from outside.
settings.readers: To the readers after 722 BC, the sermon proved that election had never been a shield.
views: Most see 3:1-15 as one unit with a short introduction and an ending on the altars.
3:1b, 3:7 and parts of 3:13-14 are seen by some as edited by a later school (Wolff, Jeremias).

title: Cows of Bashan
sum: The second sermon begins with the sharpest address in the book: "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Samaria's mountain, who squeeze the poor and crush the needy, who tell your masters, 'Bring something, so we can drink!'" The women will be dragged out of the broken wall with hooks.

Then the LORD, with a bitter joke, calls Israel to the shrines: "Go to Bethel, and rebel." The rest of the chapter is a list of five disasters (hunger, drought, blight, plague and war, and an overthrow like Sodom), each ending the same way: "yet you did not turn back to me." The sermon closes with a threat, "get ready to meet your God, Israel", and the first hymn.

views.H: Drought, blight, locusts, plague and war all appear in the records of the Near East; the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 name the same kinds of trouble (not in this order), which is probably why Amos used them. The "overthrow like Sodom" may refer to an earlier earthquake or a defeat.
views.C: 4:13 is the first of three hymns (5:8-9; 9:5-6), thought by Crenshaw to be one hymn in three parts and by Wolff to be added by a Judean school; Andersen and Freedman defend them. 4:6-11 looks like a liturgical piece, with its refrain.
views.J: The refrain "you did not turn back" fits the Jewish emphasis on teshuvah, repentance, as the aim of punishment. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra take the "cows of Bashan" as the wives of the princes; the Targum has "the wealthy of the mountain of Samaria".
views.X: "Prepare to meet your God" has been used in Christian preaching about judgment. The Greek of 4:13 ("announces to people his Christ") was used by some writers to find Christ in the hymn.
views.F: Some futurist writers apply 4:12 to the final judgment; most commentators hold that Amos speaks of a coming event in Israel's own history.

deep.b: The five disasters of 4:6-11 are the kinds of trouble the covenant curses name, though not in this order: hunger (Leviticus 26:26; Deuteronomy 28:17), drought (Deuteronomy 28:23-24), blight and locusts (Deuteronomy 28:22, 38-42), plague and war (Leviticus 26:25; Deuteronomy 28:21, 25), and overthrow (Deuteronomy 29:23). The refrain "yet you did not turn back to me" says the aim of each was repentance (1 Kings 8:33-37). When the cycle fails the LORD says, "So this is what I will do to you." What he will do is not said; the listeners must fill in the blank. That is why 4:12 is so frightening.

echoes: Leviticus 26:14-39; Deuteronomy 28; 1 Kings 8:33-37; Joel 1:4; Zechariah 3:2; Genesis 19:24-25; Exodus 19:10-17; Hosea 4:15; Psalm 22:12; Ezekiel 39:18

settings.to: Most likely the ruling-class women of Samaria first ("cows of Bashan"), then all Israel at the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal
settings.when: During the peace of Jeroboam II, probably at a festival time (the shrine offerings of 4:4-5)
settings.why: To show that the people's wealth rests on the poor, that their worship is rebellion, and that every disaster they have known was sent to bring them back. The point of the refrain is that no sign has worked, and the next step is the LORD himself.
settings.readers: The readers after 722 BC read it as an account of how the LORD tried five times before the exile.
views: The Hebrew nouns and verbs are feminine plural; the sermon is addressed to the wives of the rich (Wolff; Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra also take them as the wives of the princes).
The feminine could include all the leaders as a group of insult (some critics, with Andersen and Freedman as cautious).

title: Seek Me and Live
sum: Amos sings a funeral song for Israel while it is still alive: "She has fallen, and she will not rise again, the virgin Israel." The city that sent out a thousand men will have a hundred left. Yet the LORD says "Seek me and live", and not at Bethel, Gilgal or Beersheba, but in justice at the gate: "Hate what is evil and love what is good."

The chapter then turns on the people who long for the day of the LORD. It is darkness, not light. The LORD hates their festivals and will not listen to their songs. "Let justice roll like water, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry." The chapter closes with the question about the wilderness and an exile "beyond Damascus".

views.H: The funeral song (5:1-3) fits the period just before the Assyrian rise. The loss of nine in ten of the soldiers is the language of defeat. The gate was the courthouse (5:10, 12, 15). Pilgrimage to Beersheba from the north shows how popular these shrines were.
views.C: This chapter is the most edited. 5:8-9 is the middle hymn; 5:13 is a wisdom saying that seems out of place; 5:14-15 may be an addition because it offers hope; 5:25-27 are hard, and 5:26 may be a gloss with the names of Assyrian gods. The vocabulary of "seek" is shared with Deuteronomy.
views.J: The Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) tells of the commandments being reduced to "Seek me and live" (Amos) and "the righteous will live by his faith" (Habakkuk). The Damascus Document at Qumran cites 5:26-27. Rashi reads "Seek me and live" (5:4) as a call to the pilgrimage to Jerusalem; on 5:24 he follows the Targum, "the justice you have hidden will be revealed like water", while Radak and Ibn Ezra say the LORD wants justice, not sacrifice and song. On 5:25 Rashi says Israel offered only the Passover in the wilderness (from the Sifre), whereas Radak and Ibn Ezra report the tradition that the Levites offered.
views.X: Stephen quotes 5:25-27 in Acts 7:42-43. Martin Luther King Jr. used 5:24 in 1963; the social gospel, Catholic social teaching and liberation theology make 5:21-24 a central text.
views.F: Dispensational and other futurist readers take the "day of the LORD" (5:18-20) as the final day; others hold that for Amos it is the coming of Assyria; the New Testament uses the phrase for the return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 5:2).

deep.b:
5:21-24 is the best-known part of the book, and it needs to be read with care. The LORD "hates" (sana'ti) the festivals, offerings and songs. It is not that sacrifice is wrong; Israel's law commands it. It is that worship and wrongdoing cannot be offered together (Isaiah 1:11-17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8; Psalm 50). Amos does not say what to do with the sacrifices, only what is to flow: justice and righteousness. The picture is of what the prophet wants: a steady stream (nachal 'eitan) in place of the flash flood of festival days.

The Hebrew words are mishpat and tsedaqah. Mishpat is the decision of the court, and the order of a community in which the weak are protected; tsedaqah is the right conduct toward others. They are always together in the prophets. English "justice" and "righteousness" are not exact, and "social justice" is a modern phrase that the Hebrew does not have, but the concern is the same: how the weak are treated by the strong.

5:26 is one of the hardest verses in the book. The Hebrew has two names, Sikkuth and Kiyyun, which look like the names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Sakkuth, a title of Ninurta, and Kajamanu, Saturn). The vowels of the first may be those of shiqquts, "abomination". The Greek reads "the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan", and Acts 7:43 follows the Greek, and puts Babylon where the Hebrew has Damascus. The Damascus Document (CD 7) reads the first word as sukkat, "booth", and explains the booth as the books of the Law and Kiyyun as the books of the prophets. The Plain keeps the Hebrew names, and the notes give each reading.

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13; Isaiah 1:11-17; Isaiah 58; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8; Job 9:9; Job 38:31; Joel 1:15; Zephaniah 1:14-18; Acts 7:42-43; Habakkuk 2:4; Leviticus 26:31; Exodus 12:12

traditions.q: What the text raises today: is working for social justice part of the church's mission? (5:21-24; 2:6-8)
views: Yes. Love for the poor and works of justice belong to the Christian life and cannot be separated from worship (Catechism 2443-2449). The Church's social teaching treats the prophets, including Amos, as a root of this.

Yes, and it begins with the law: Calvin reads the second table of the commandments as requiring help for the neighbor and not only keeping from harm (Institutes 2.8). Reformed churches differ on whether this work belongs to the church as a body or to its members in their callings.

God rules the world through civil government and law, which keep order and justice, and the church through the gospel. Christians serve justice in their callings in the world (Augsburg Confession XVI), while the church's own task is the gospel and the sacraments (Augsburg Confession VII).

Christians are to work to make Christ's will supreme in society, to oppose greed and racism, and to care for the orphaned, needy, abused, aged and sick (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article XV), while the church's first mission is evangelism (Article XI).

The church is called to be a community of peace and shared goods whose own life shows what justice is, and which is not conformed to the powers of the world (Mennonite Confession of Faith, 1995, on the church and on peace and justice).
Orthodox teaching ties the Eucharist to care for the poor, so that worship and justice are not separate (a short summary; no source is cited).

settings.what: A lament and a call to seek the LORD
settings.to: The house of Israel, and in particular those who go to Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba and those who sit in the gate
settings.when: During the peace of Jeroboam II
settings.why: To sing a funeral song over a nation that thinks it is safe, and in the same breath to say that there is still a way: seek the LORD, and let justice stand in the gate. The listener has to hear both.
settings.readers: Those who read it after 722 BC heard the lament as already fulfilled and the invitation as a call to those who remained.
views: Most see 5:1-6 and 5:10-12 as Amos; 5:14-15 is the debated one.
Wolff and Jeremias suggest 5:14-15 and 5:13 came later, because they offer a way out the lament does not.

settings.what: A woe on those who long for the day of the LORD, and on their festivals
settings.to: The worshippers at the northern shrines, who expect the day of the LORD to rescue them
settings.when: During a festival or a pilgrimage season; the content fits the pilgrim feasts of 5:21
settings.why: To take away a hope that was widely held, and to show that the LORD does not accept worship while justice is absent. The reference to the forty wilderness years makes the point that the relationship was never based on sacrifice alone.
settings.readers: Later readers in exile read the passage as an explanation of why the shrines were gone.
views: Day of the LORD as national hope
Wolff, Paul: the people expected a victory day.
Day of the LORD as festival
Mowinckel: an enthronement festival that Amos reverses.

title: Woe to the Comfortable
sum: The third sermon is a "woe" on the leaders who are at ease in Zion and secure on Samaria's mountain. They lie on ivory beds, eat lamb and fattened calf, make up songs like David and drink wine by the bowlful, but "the ruin of Joseph does not make them sick". They will go into exile first.

The LORD swears by himself that he loathes the pride of Jacob and will hand over the city. A scene of the dead in the house follows, with a man asking "Is anyone still with you?" and the answer, "No." The chapter ends with two impossible questions about horses on a cliff, the boast about Lo-debar and Karnaim, and a warning that a nation will squeeze Israel from Lebo-hamath to the wadi of the Arabah.

views.H: The border Jeroboam II had won (2 Kings 14:25) is turned against him: the invader will take it back. The "nation" is Assyria, never named. Calneh, Hamath and Gath fell to Assyria after Amos's day (Tiglath-pileser III, 738 BC; Sargon II, 720 and about 712 BC), so 6:2 is read either as a later addition or as naming earlier events (see the note); the Greek has no Calneh.
views.C: "In Zion" (6:1), the cities of 6:2 and "the nation" of 6:14 are seen by some as later touches. The text of 6:10 and 6:12 is hard. 6:9-10 is prose in the middle of poetry.
views.X: The chapter has often been preached against complacency in the church. The social gospel and liberation writers use 6:4-7.
views.F: Some dispensational readers see in 6:14 the nation of Assyria only; futurist readings of the verse are rare.
views.J: Radak reads the woe of 6:1 as falling on the rich of both capitals, Zion and Samaria, who feel no grief over the exile of Israel. Ibn Ezra takes "Woe" as a sign of the exile under Nebuchadnezzar. Rashi takes "the first of the nations" as "the most praiseworthy of the nations" and "the house of Israel comes to them" as Israel choosing the ways of the nations.

echoes: Isaiah 5:11-12; Isaiah 32:9-11; Jeremiah 16:5; 2 Kings 14:25; Amos 3:15; Amos 5:7; Amos 8:7; Hosea 10:4; 2 Samuel 9:4

deep.b: The two questions of 6:12 are unusual: horses do not run on a cliff, and oxen do not plow rock. The Greek makes the second question "Will they be silent among mares?", and some modern scholars change the Hebrew to "plow the sea with oxen". Either way the verse says that what Israel has done, turning justice into poison, is as unnatural as these things. Lo-debar and Karnaim are towns across the Jordan that Israel had taken back. Their names are puns ("Nothing" and "Horns"), so the boast is that with their strength they have taken a Nothing. The reply in 6:14 sets the limits of their conquest as the limits of their defeat.

settings.what: The third sermon, a woe on the comfortable
settings.to: Possibly the leaders of Samaria and Zion, "the famous men of the first of the nations", and the people who come to them
settings.when: During the years of peace, with the luxuries of 6:4-6 as the target
settings.why: To strip away the leaders' sense of safety. Their ease depends on a security that does not exist; they will lead the line into exile.
settings.readers: Readers after 722 BC read 6:7 as a description of what happened.
views: Some think "in Zion" is a Judean touch (Wolff).
Paul and others see Amos as addressing both kingdoms. Radak reads the woe as falling on the rich of both Zion and Samaria; Ibn Ezra takes the woe on Zion as a sign of the exile under Nebuchadnezzar.

title: Locusts, Fire and the Plumb Line
sum: The visions begin. In the first, the Lord GOD forms a swarm of locusts. In the second, a fire eats up the great deep and the farmland. Each time Amos asks, "Please forgive! Small as he is, how will Jacob get up?" and each time "the LORD changed his mind about this". The third vision is a wall and a plumb line, and now there is no prayer: "I will not overlook them any more."

Then the story breaks in. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to the king and tells him to go back to Judah and earn his bread there. Amos answers: "I am no prophet, and I am no prophet's son. I am a herdsman, and I tend sycamore figs." The LORD took him from the flock and told him to prophesy. Amaziah's family will pay for his order.

views.H: Amos is at Bethel, the king's sanctuary. The priest speaks as a royal official. The fate of Jeroboam's house (2 Kings 15:8-12) is the nearest fulfilment of 7:9; 7:11's "Jeroboam will die by the sword" is not in 2 Kings 14:29, and the Plain does not harmonize them.
views.C: The vision report (7:1-9) and the Amaziah story (7:10-17) are different forms: the first is the prophet's first-person report and the second is third-person narrative about him until 7:14. Most scholars think the story was inserted at 7:10 to explain why the visions were spoken at Bethel. The word 'anak in 7:7-8 is unique.
views.X: 7:10-17 is cited for the prophet's freedom from the state and the minister's call from God.
views.F: Few futurist readings apply; the visions are tied to the reign of Jeroboam II.
views.J: Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra and the Targum read "the king's mowings" (7:1) as the first cutting taken for the king's animals (Rashi and the Targum: the king's young grain, mown as fodder). On 7:14 the medieval readings divide on the tense: Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as "I was no prophet", while Rashi, following the Targum, has Amos deny being a paid prophet, since he was a wealthy owner of cattle.

deep.h: The three visions and the prayer
deep.b:
The first two visions follow the same pattern: "The Lord GOD showed me this" ... a catastrophe in the making ... Amos's prayer ... "The LORD changed his mind about this." The third vision breaks the pattern: there is no prayer, because the LORD has already said, "I will not overlook them any more." Intercession works twice and then it is over. This is how Jeremiah is forbidden to pray (Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14; 14:11), while Moses' prayer is heard even after the worst failures (Exodus 32:14; Numbers 14:20), though in Numbers 14 that generation still dies in the wilderness (14:22-23).

The question of whether God really changed his mind is an old one. The Plain uses the same English as the site's Exodus 32:14 and Jeremiah 18:8 (see the topic on God's change of mind). Whatever the explanation, the story assumes that the prophet's prayer is not empty: it changed what was announced.

deep.h: Amos and Amaziah: "I am no prophet"
deep.b: Amaziah calls Amos a "seer" and tells him to take his prophesying to Judah, "and eat bread there". The priest assumes prophets are paid. Amos replies that he is no prophet by trade and not a member of a prophetic guild. The Hebrew has no verb, so both "I am" and "I was" are possible. If "I am", Amos refuses the label while still doing the work. If "I was", he is telling Amaziah that he used to be a herdsman until the LORD took him. Either way the claim is the same: the authority comes from the LORD's order ("Go, prophesy") and not from the office. See the entry on the variants for the Greek and the Latin.

echoes: Exodus 32:11-14; Numbers 14:13-19; Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 14:11; Joel 2:13-14; Jonah 3:9-10; 2 Kings 14:23-29; 2 Kings 15:8-12; 1 Kings 12:31-33; 2 Samuel 7:8; Zechariah 13:5

traditions.q: Does God really change his mind? (7:3, 6)
views: The Bible's language of God "repenting" is a way of speaking to human weakness. God is "without body, parts, or passions, immutable" (Westminster Confession 2.1); Calvin teaches that such language describes a change in how God deals with people, not a change in his purpose (Institutes 1.17.12-13).

God's will does not change (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 19, a. 7). The language of relenting is human speech about a God who acts in time, and prayer matters because God has willed that certain things happen through prayer (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 83, a. 2).

God is unchanging in his nature (John of Damascus, Exposition of the Orthodox Faith); the passages of "repentance" are God's condescension to human speech, and the Fathers hold that repentance and prayer truly change what happens to people.

Prayer is commanded and God has promised to hear it (Luther, Large Catechism, on the Lord's Prayer), so the church prays as Amos does, trusting the promise. There is no single Lutheran statement on the "changed his mind" verses (a short summary).

In the Wesleyan tradition God truly responds to human prayer and repentance without any change in his character; his foreknowledge does not remove human freedom. (Wesley does not comment on Amos; this applies his teaching that God works in us and we respond.)

settings.by: Amos, reporting what the Lord GOD "showed" him
settings.to: The prophet's hearers at Bethel (and the readers of the book); the vision is addressed to Amos himself
settings.when: In the reign of Jeroboam II, before the Amaziah scene, perhaps at Bethel
settings.why: To say, in three pictures, that the LORD held back judgment twice at the prophet's prayer and then would not. The prayer shows that the prophet is on Israel's side; the third vision shows that the time is up.
settings.readers: Later readers read the visions as the record of a patience that ended with 722 BC.
views: Many commentators take them as visionary experiences (Wolff, Paul).
Some see them as a way of presenting oracles as visions.

settings.by: Amaziah the priest, and Amos, as the story reports
settings.to: Amaziah to Jeroboam and to Amos; Amos to Amaziah and his family
settings.when: At Bethel, "the king's sanctuary", on a day when Amos was prophesying there
settings.why: To show that the book's words were spoken against an official attempt to silence them, and that the prophet's authority does not rest on a guild or a payroll. For the first readers, the story explained why Amos left and what became of the priest's family.
settings.readers: The readers after 722 BC read the final prophecy against Amaziah as already fulfilled.
views: Most take it as a real confrontation (Hayes, Paul).
The story is told in the third person and is seen as a later narrative (Wolff).

title: Summer Fruit
sum: The fourth vision is a basket of summer fruit. In Hebrew qayits ("summer fruit") sounds like qets ("end"), and the LORD says, "The end has come for my people Israel." The songs of the temple will turn to wailing. Then Amos turns on the merchants who wait for the New Moon and the Sabbath to pass so that they can sell grain with small measures and rigged scales, "buying the poor for silver and the needy for the price of a pair of sandals".

The LORD swears never to forget their deeds. The land will shake, the sun will go down at midday, festivals will turn into mourning "like the grief over an only son", and there will be a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the words of the LORD. The beautiful young women and young men will faint, and those who swear by Dan and Beersheba will fall and not rise.

views.H: Trade in grain in the 8th century was a path to land: debt, sale of people, loss of fields. Sabbath and New Moon are evidence for the observance of rest days. The "sun at noon" may recall the eclipse of 763 BC, but this is not proved.
views.C: 8:4-14 has been edited more than once: 8:8-14 contains several short sayings, some with "on that day". 8:11-12 is sometimes seen as an addition from a later time of prophetic silence. The Ketiv and Qere in 8:4 and 8:8 are minor.
views.X: 8:9 has been linked to the darkness at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:45), and 8:11 to the church's need for preaching.
views.F: Futurist readers apply 8:9-10 to the end-time signs of the day of the LORD, together with Joel 2:31 and Revelation 6:12; others keep it as 8th-century language.
views.J: Rashi reads the "basket of summer fruit" as a basket of late figs, which are not good fruit. Ibn Ezra's short gloss on 8:2 plays on the same sound, with "your end" and "your harvest".

echoes: Ezekiel 7:2-6; Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Micah 6:10-11; Proverbs 11:1; Nehemiah 13:15-22; Exodus 20:8-11; Matthew 27:45; Matthew 4:4; 1 Samuel 3:1; Amos 2:6

settings.by: Amos, reporting a vision from the Lord GOD
settings.when: Likely at the same time as the other visions in 7:1-9
settings.why: To announce, with a pun, that the time is ripe: the fruit is ripe, the end has come. There is no prayer, and no change of mind.
settings.readers: Later readers saw in the pun a single word for the fall of Samaria.

settings.what: The oracle against the merchants and the coming silence
settings.to: The grain merchants and powerful who buy and sell the poor; then all the land
settings.when: On days around the New Moon and the Sabbath, with a market in the background
settings.why: To name the exact tricks (small measure, heavy weight, rigged scales, sweepings sold as wheat) and to say the LORD has sworn not to forget. The set of images that follows (earthquake, black noon, mourning, hunger for the word) takes the listeners from the market to the day of the LORD.
settings.readers: Readers after the fall of Samaria saw the famine of the word in the years when no prophet spoke.
views: 8:4-8 are widely accepted; 8:9-14 are more argued (Wolff, Paul).
8:9-14 seems a series of short sayings joined by "on that day" (Jeremias).

title: The Fallen Booth
sum: The fifth vision shows the Lord standing over the altar and ordering the capitals struck so that the building falls on the heads of the people. No one can escape: not into Sheol, not to the heavens, not to Carmel, not to the bottom of the sea, not into captivity. After the third hymn, the LORD asks, "Are you Israelites not like the Cushites to me?" He brought up Israel from Egypt, but also the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir. The sinful kingdom will be wiped off the face of the ground, yet not the house of Jacob completely. The sinners will be shaken in a sieve and die.

Then the last five verses turn to hope: "On that day I will set up again the fallen booth of David." The nations called by the LORD's name are included. The plowman will catch up with the reaper, the mountains will drip sweet wine, and Israel will be planted in its own soil and never again torn up.

views.H: The fifth vision is the end of the northern kingdom's hope. The epilogue assumes a fallen house of David, and is dated by many to after 586 BC (the fall of the Davidic line) or to the time of Josiah (when the north was a hope to reunite); others keep it for Amos.
views.C: The usual critical view (Wolff, Jeremias) is that 9:8b-15 or 9:11-15 was added after the exile, because it assumes a fallen Davidic house and ends the book on hope. Paul, Hayes and Andersen-Freedman argue for Amos as the author, or for an early Judean edition. 9:5-6 is the third hymn, and 9:7 is a universalizing verse.
views.J: The Targum Jonathan reads the "booth of David" as the kingdom of the house of David, and Rashi quotes it; Radak reads the booth as David's kingdom raised on the day of redemption. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 96b-97a) uses 9:11 to call the Messiah Bar Nafle, "son of the fallen". The Damascus Document (CD 7) explains the "booth of the king" of 5:26 as the books of the Law and quotes 9:11 nearby, and 4QFlorilegium reads "the booth of David" of the Branch of David. On 9:12 Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra read the verse as turned around, so that Israel possesses the remnant of Edom and the nations (Ibn Ezra: after Sennacherib's death, or, if of the Messiah, clearly so). On 9:13 Rashi sees Leviticus 26:5, and Radak notes that "milk" is to be supplied from Joel 3:18.
views.X: Acts 15:16-18 quotes 9:11-12 in the Greek form, with changes of its own at the start: "that those who are left of humankind may seek out the Lord". Christian readers have read the "booth" as fulfilled in Christ and the church of Jews and Gentiles, or as still to come. 9:7 is cited for God's care for all peoples.
views.F: Dispensational readers expect the literal restoration of Israel after the church age (Acts 15:16, "after these things I will come back", which is the wording of Acts: Amos 9:11 has "on that day" in Hebrew and in Greek), amillennial ones read the promises of land and harvest as the church or the new creation, and progressive dispensationalists see David's throne restored in Christ now with Israel's promises still to come (Bock). Jewish readers see the return and the Messiah.

deep.h: Edom or humankind? Hebrew and Greek in 9:12
deep.b:
The Hebrew of 9:12 says that David's booth will be raised "so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by my name". The Greek has "so that the rest of humankind may seek, and all the nations over whom my name is called", and that is what James quotes in Acts 15:16-18 to support receiving Gentiles who turn to God. The two texts differ by two small things: yirshu "possess" against yidreshu "seek" (a letter d), and Edom (aleph-dalet-vav-mem) against adam "humankind" (aleph-dalet-mem), a vowel letter often not written.

Three explanations are held by good scholars. (1) The Greek translator had a Hebrew text that read "seek" and "humankind"; the Hebrew we have would then be a later change. (2) The Greek translator, with the Masoretic text before him, read the consonants with other vowels and so turned a promise of conquest into a promise of conversion. (3) James used the Greek because it was the text of his hearers (the Council met in Jerusalem, but the quotation is in the Greek of Acts); his argument leans on "the nations over whom my name is called", which is in both, and on the agreement of "the words of the prophets". Of the scrolls, Mur88 (MurXII) has "the remnant of Edom" with the word "Edom" intact, but the verb "possess" is a restored word and cannot be cited. The Plain follows the Hebrew and gives the Greek as a variant.

deep.title: Raised, not rebuilt
deep.b: My own observation: Amos never says "rebuild" in 9:11 without also saying "raise up" (hqim). The verb "raise up" is the same verb as the one used for Jacob's question in 7:2, 5 ("how will Jacob get up?", qum, in its intransitive form) and for the fall in 5:2 ("she will not rise again"). So the book brackets its theme with a verb: the virgin Israel "will not rise" (5:2), Jacob cannot "rise" (7:2, 5), the sinners "will fall and never get up again" (8:14), and at the end the LORD himself "raises" the fallen booth (9:11). This is a pattern of one root through the book. It overlaps with the literary readings of Paul and Andersen-Freedman, but I do not know of a published argument that makes it the book's plan.

echoes: Acts 15:15-18; Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 37:15-28; Jeremiah 30:3; Jeremiah 24:6; Joel 3:18; Obadiah 19-21; Leviticus 26:5; Isaiah 25:6; Psalm 139:7-12; Jeremiah 13:23; Deuteronomy 2:23; 2 Samuel 7

traditions.q: What does James mean in Acts 15 by quoting Amos 9:11-12, and what is the "booth of David"?
views: Acts 15 shows the Church as the restored house of David, which includes believing Gentiles. Lumen Gentium 9 describes the new People of God as drawn from Jews and Gentiles, and Nostra Aetate 4 teaches that God's call to the Jewish people has not been revoked. (Lumen Gentium 9 and Nostra Aetate 4 are general statements on the people of God and on the Jewish people; neither comments on Acts 15, and no Catholic commentary on Amos 9:11 has been checked for this card.)
Calvin reads the fallen "tent of David" as David's royal house raised up in Christ and gathered into the church from Jews and Gentiles; the promise is already being fulfilled (Commentary on Acts 15).

James quotes Amos only to show that the Gentile blessing agrees with the prophets. "After these things I will come back" (Acts 15:16, which is Acts's wording and not Amos's) places the rebuilding of David's booth in the future kingdom after Christ returns, and the promises to Israel in Amos 9:13-15 remain for Israel (Scofield; Ryrie).

Chrysostom, in his homily on Acts 15, reads James's quotation as proof from the prophets that the nations come to God without circumcision (a short summary; his own words on Amos 9:11 were not checked).

Progressive dispensational writers (Blaising and Bock) hold that David's throne is restored now in Christ's enthronement, which already brings Gentiles in, while the promises to national Israel are still to be completed.

settings.what: The fifth vision and the verdict
settings.by: Amos, reporting what he saw; the LORD speaks in the first person
settings.to: The people of Israel (and the readers of the book)
settings.when: At the end of the visions, in the reign of Jeroboam II; the place is the altar of the shrine (possibly Bethel)
settings.why: To close every door: there is no refuge, not even in the shrine. The strike at the building is followed by a statement that Israel is not above the other nations (9:7) and a sentence on the sinners (9:10), who say that disaster will not touch them.
settings.readers: Readers after 722 BC read the vision as an account of the fall of Samaria and the exile.
views: Many see the altar as Bethel's (Wolff, Paul).

settings.by: The LORD, through Amos or a later editor
settings.to: Possibly the people after judgment: the survivors of Israel and Judah, and the nations called by the LORD's name
settings.when: "On that day", after the disaster: for the first readers the time after the exile
settings.why: To say that the last word is not judgment. For readers who knew the booth had fallen, the promise is that the LORD himself will raise it, and the land and the harvest will be given back.
settings.readers: Readers after 586 BC read it as the promise of return; later Jews and Christians read it as messianic.
views: Paul, Hayes, Andersen-Freedman: Amos could end on hope.
Wolff, Jeremias: it presupposes the fall of the Davidic house.
